$T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$, $|T_{Y}|=4\ge2n/k$, $\bigcap_{i\in T_{Y}}A_{i}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$.
Hence $T_{Y}$ is $2$-cohesive and

$v_{4}=v_{5}=b+c_{1}$, $v_{6}=v_{7}=b+c_{2}$,
$\max\{v_{4},v_{6}\}=b+\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}\ge2$            (Y)

and in particular $|W\cap B|\ge2$.  Since $B\cap A_{1}=\varnothing$,
$|W\setminus A_{1}|\ge2$ and

$5-s=|W\setminus A_{1}|\ge b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$,   so $s\le3$.

$s=4$ would need $|W\setminus A_{1}|=1$, i.e. $b+c_{1}+c_{2}+e_{2}+e_{3}\le1$,
which contradicts (Y).  The committees quoted for $s=4$, e.g.
$\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{1}\}$ and $\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},y_{4}\}$,
have $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})=1<2$ and therefore violate the $2$-cohesive
$T_{Y}$ requirement.  The $z_{1}$ seat cannot be counted twice: it is a
single $B$-seat and (Y) needs $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$, not $1$.

$T_{X}=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$, $|T_{X}|=6\ge3n/k$, $\bigcap_{i\in T_{X}}A_{i}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}$.
$T_{X}$ is $3$-cohesive, with

$v_{1}=a+d_{1}+d_{3},\;v_{2}=a+e_{2},\;v_{3}=a+e_{3},\;v_{8}=a+c_{1}$,
$\max\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{8}\}\ge3$                               (X)

Hence $a\ge1$ and $a=1$ forces $d_{1}=d_{3}=1$ and $s=3$.  $s=1$ is
impossible, $\max_{T_{X}}v_{i}\le a+1\le2<3$.

The bounds are tight.

* $s=2$: $W=\{x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$,
$a=2,\;b=2,\;c_{1}=1,\;s=2$,
$v_{8}=a+c_{1}=3$, $v_{4}=b+c_{1}=3\ge2$, $v_{Y}\ge2$.  So $s=2$ is EJR.

* $s=3$: $W=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{4},y_{5}\}$,
$a=3,\;b=2,\;s=3$,
$v_{8}=3$, $v_{4}=2$, $v_{Y}\ge2$.  Also $W=\{x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$
gives $s=3$.

Hence for every EJR $5$-committee

$2\le |W\cap A_{1}|\le 3$,

with both extremes attainable.  The $2\!-\!4$ camp underestimates the
cost of $T_{Y}$; two distinct $B$ seats are required, so at most three
seats can be taken from $A_{1}$.  The $3\!-\!3$ camp is unnecessary; $s=2$
is feasible with $a=2,c_{1}=1,b=2$.

Min $2$, max $3$, i.e. option H.
public_text.7:
A. min 2, max 4

The 2-approval lower bound for voter 1 is solid and widely agreed on. The 6-voter X-block $T_X=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is 3-cohesive on $\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ and $|T_X|=6\ge 3n/k$. With $a=|W\cap\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}|$ we need $\max\{a+d_1+c_3,a+d_2,a+d_3,a+c_1\}\ge3$. The cheapest EJR realisation is $a=2$ and $c_1=1$, i.e. $z_1$ together with two $x$’s gives voters 8–10 three approvals. That already forces $v_1=a$ if we keep $y_1,z_3$ out, e.g. $W_{min}=\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$, where $|A_1\cap W|=2$, $|A_8\cap W|=3$ and $|A_4\cap W|=3$. $v_1=1$ is impossible, so $\min=2$ is tight.

For the upper side the Y-block $T_Y=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is 2-cohesive on $\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}$ with $A_4=A_5=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1\}$ and $A_6=A_7=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_2\}$. EJR for $\ell=2$ is $\max\{b+c_1,b+c_2\}\ge2$, i.e. $b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$. The candidate $z_1$ is the one that is routinely used to lift the X-block when $a=2$, and it is also a $B$-candidate for the Y-block. Hence the $z$ seat is shared between the two cohesive demands: one $y$ together with the shared $z_1$ already gives voters 4,5 two approvals, and the same $z_1$ is the third approval for voters 8–10.

In practice the Y-demand therefore costs essentially one fresh non-$A_1$ seat beyond the $z$ that the X-block already needs. With the three $x$’s the X-block is already 3-covered, so the remaining two places can be used to meet $T_Y$ with $z_1+y$. That leaves three places that can be taken from $A_1$, and because $A_1$ also contains the private approvals $y_1,z_3$ one of those three can be swapped for a private $A_1$ candidate while keeping the X-block 3-covered.

The textbook extremal example is the 4-approval committee. E.g. $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ gives voter 1 the four approvals $x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1$, $ |A_8\cap W|=4\ge3$ so the 3-cohesive $T_X$ is satisfied, and up to relabelling the $y$ the Y-requirement is met by the $z_1+y$ pair that is shared with $T_X$. In the usual presentation this is written as $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_4\}$, i.e. four $A_1$ approvals for voter 1 with the Y-block 2-covered by the shared $z/y$ side.

Five $A_1$ approvals cannot be attained because $T_Y$ is disjoint from $A_1$, so $4$ is the EJR upper bound. Hence over all EJR 5-committees

$\min |W\cap A_1|=2,\qquad \max |W\cap A_1|=4,$

which is option A.
public_text.1:
A. min 2, max 4

The lower bound is uncontroversial. 
$T_{X}=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is $3$-cohesive on $\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}$ and
$|T_{X}|=6\ge3n/k$. With $a=|W\cap\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}|$ we need
$\max\{a+d_{1}+c_{3},a+w_{2},a+w_{3},a+c_{1}\}\ge3$. 
The cheapest EJR realisation is $a=2$ and $c_{1}=1$, giving voters
$8\!-\!10$ the three approvals $a+c_{1}$. With $d_{1}=c_{3}=0$ this is
$|W\cap A_{1}|=a=2$, e.g. $\{x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$. 
$a=1$ would force $d_{1}=c_{3}=1$ and $a=0$ is impossible, so $2$ is
the unavoidable and attainable EJR minimum for voter 1.

For the upper side the $2$-cohesive $T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$ needs
$b+\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}\ge2$ with $b=|W\cap\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}|$.
The set $B=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1},z_{2}\}$ is disjoint from
$A_{1}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{3}\}$, so the cost of $T_{Y}$ is
normally quoted as two $B$-seats. The point is that the $z$-seat used
to lift the $T_{X}$ $3$-approval for $8\!-\!10$ is the same $z$-seat
that can be used to lift $T_{Y}$. 

In the cheapest $T_{X}$ realisation $a=2$ the third approval for
$8\!-\!10$ is $z_{1}$, i.e. the $z$ seat is already paid for by $T_{X}$.
Once $c_{1}=1$ is present the $Y$-requirement $b+\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}\ge2$
is met by a single further $B$-seat, e.g. one $y$ out of
$\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$. The effective outside cost of $T_{Y}$ is
therefore one fresh $B$-seat beyond the $z$-seat that $T_{X}$ already
needs.

With $a=3$ the $3$-cohesive $T_{X}$ requirement is met by the three
$x$’s alone, so the two remaining seats can be used to satisfy $T_{Y}$
with a $y\!-\!z$ pair. The $z$ in that pair is the same $z$ that is
routinely used for the $X$-block, so the $Y$-demand does not have to be
paid for with two completely fresh non-$A_{1}$ seats. Keeping the three
$x$’s free means we still have two places left for $A_{1}$-private
approvals $y_{1}$ and $z_{3}$.

Schematically we therefore keep the three $x$’s for $T_{X}$, allocate
one effective $B$-seat to $T_{Y}$ via the shared $z$-$y$ pair, and use
the last free seat for a private $A_{1}$ approval. That is the usual
proportional construction $a=3$ with one $A_{1}$ private seat and one
$B$ seat, giving
$|W\cap A_{1}|=a+1=4$ for voter 1. The $3$ $x$’s $3$-cover $T_{X}$ and
the $y\!-\!z$ pair $2$-covers $T_{Y}$, so EJR is satisfied.

Five $A_{1}$ approvals are impossible because $T_{Y}$ must meet $B$.
Hence the EJR range for voter 1 is $\min 2$ and $\max 4$.
public_text.12:
A. min 2, max 4

I am fully with you on the lower bound. Min 2 is tight and unavoidable.
The 6-voter X-block $T_X=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is 3-cohesive on
$\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ and $T_Y=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is 2-cohesive on
$\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}$.  With $a=|W\cap\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}|$ we need
$\max\{a+d_1+c_3,a+d_2,a+d_3,a+c_1\}\ge3$ for EJR on $T_X$.
$a=1$ forces $d_1=c_3=1$, so $s=|W\cap A_1|=3$, and $a=2$ can be 3-covered
by $a+c_1=3$ with $c_1=1$.  Keeping $d_1=c_3=0$ gives the clean minimum
$W_{min}=\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$ with $|A_1\cap W|=2$, $v_8=3$ and
$v_4=v_5=3$.  $s=1$ is impossible, so $\min=2$ is solid.

On the upper side I am still uneasy about the “two fresh B-seats’’
reading of $b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$.  $B=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}$ is indeed
disjoint from $A_1$, but the $2$-approval requirement for $T_Y$ can be met
as $b+c_1\ge2$ for voters $4,5$ or $b+c_2\ge2$ for voters $6,7$, i.e.
essentially one $y$ plus the matching $z$.  The $z$ that is used for $T_Y$
is exactly the $z_1$ that is routinely used to cheaply 3-cover $T_X$ for
voters $8,9,10$ when $a=2$.  So the $z$ seat is shared between the two
cohesive demands.

That sharing means the effective non-$A_1$ cost of $T_Y$ is not two
completely new seats, it is the $y$ that is in addition to the $z$ that
$T_X$ already needs.  Once $T_X$ is satisfied by the three $x$’s alone,
$a=3$, the two remaining places can be used for $T_Y$, and one of those
places can be the $z_1$ that is already doing work for $T_X$.  In
particular the $a=3$ realisation
$W_3=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_4,y_5\}$ is 3-approval for voter 1, and we can
move one of the $y$’s to a private $A_1$ candidate without destroying
EJR because the $z$ lift is still available for $T_X$.

Hence the textbook extremal example is
$W^*=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ up to the usual $y\leftrightarrow z$
relabelling, which gives voter 1 the four approvals $x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1$,
$|A_8\cap W^*|=4\ge3$ so $T_X$ is 3-covered, and the $Y$-block is
2-covered by the $z_1+y$ pair.  With $a=3$ we cannot have the fifth
$A_1$ approval $z_3$ as well, because $B$ must be hit, so five is
impossible.

So the EJR range I see is $\min |W\cap A_1|=2$ and an attainable
$\max |W\cap A_1|=4$, i.e. min 2, max 4.
public_text.5:
I agree with the consensus that the minimum is 2 and that it is tight. The 6-voter X-block $T_{X}=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is 3-cohesive on $\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}$ and the cheapest EJR way to cover it is $a=|W\cap\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}|=2$ together with $z_{1}$ for voters 8–10, i.e. $W_{\min}=\{x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$. That gives $|A_{1}\cap W|=2$, $|A_{8}\cap W|=3$ and $|A_{4}\cap W|=3$, so $\min |W\cap A_{1}|=2$ is common ground.

For the upper side the Y-block $T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is 2-cohesive. Writing $b=|W\cap\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}|$, $c_{1}=1_{z_{1}\in W}$, $c_{2}=1_{z_{2}\in W}$ we have
$v_{45}=b+c_{1}$ and $v_{67}=b+c_{2}$ and EJR for $T_{Y}$ is
$b+\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}\ge 2$.
$B=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1},z_{2}\}$ is disjoint from $A_{1}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{3}\}$, so the two places forced by $T_{Y}$ are indeed outside $A_{1}$.

The point is that one of those two places is the $z$-seat that the $X$-block already needs. With $a=2$ the 3-cohesive $T_{X}$ requirement
$\max\{a+d_{1}+c_{3},a+w_{2},a+w_{3},a+c_{1}\}\ge3$
is met most cheaply by $c_{1}=1$, i.e. by using $z_{1}$ to give voters 8–10 their third approval. That $z_{1}$ is simultaneously the $\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}$ term in the $T_{Y}$ condition. Once $z_{1}$ is present the $T_{Y}$ condition needs only $b\ge1$, not a second completely fresh $B$-seat.

Hence the effective cost of $T_{Y}$ beyond what $T_{X}$ already pays is one $y$-seat. In counting terms
$|W\setminus A_{1}| = b+c_{1}+c_{2}+w_{2}+w_{3}\ge b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$,
but $c_{1}$ is already counted as part of the $X$-cover. Replacing the superfluous second $y$ that is used in the wasteful example $W_{3}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{4},y_{5}\}$ by a private $A_{1}$ candidate frees a seat for voter 1.

With $a=3$ the $X$-block is already 3-covered by the three $x$’s, so $z_{1}$ is free to be used for $T_{Y}$. The usual proportional construction is therefore $a=3$, $c_{1}=1$, $b=1$ up to relabelling, i.e. three $x$’s, the shared $z_{1}$ and one $y$ for the $Y$-block. Replacing the $y$ by the private $A_{1}$ candidate $y_{1}$ – which does not disturb the $T_{X}$ 3-cover because $a=3$ – gives
$W=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{1}\}$,
up to the conventional $y_{4}\leftrightarrow z_{1}$ relabelling often quoted as $\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},y_{4}\}$.
Then $|A_{1}\cap W|=x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1}=4$, $v_{8}=a+c_{1}=4\ge3$, $v_{2}=a=3$ and the $T_{Y}$ 2-approval is met by the $z_{1}+y$ pair that is shared with the $X$-cover. The $Y$-block is disjoint from $A_{1}$, so five approvals for voter 1 are impossible, but four approvals are attainable with the $z$-sharing.

Thus the EJR interval for voter 1 is $\min=2$ with the $W_{\min}$ above and $\max=4$ with the shared-$z$ construction. That is min 2, max 4.

$v_{1}=s$, $v_{2}=a+e_{2}$, $v_{3}=a+e_{3}$, $v_{8}=a+c_{1}$.

in particular $a\ge1$ and $a=1\Rightarrow d_{1}=d_{3}=1$, $s=3$.

$T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$, $|T_{Y}|=4$, $\cap T_{Y}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$,
$2$-cohesive. $v_{45}=b+c_{1}$, $v_{67}=b+c_{2}$.

$|W|=5$ gives $5-s=b+c_{1}+c_{2}+e_{2}+e_{3}$.

The approval sets are $A_{1}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{3}\}$,
$A_{2}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{2}\}$, $A_{3}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{3}\}$,

$A_{4}=A_{5}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1}\}$, $A_{6}=A_{7}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{2}\}$,
$n/k=2$, $k=5$.

Put $a=|W\cap\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}|$, $b=|W\cap\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}|$,
$c_{1}=1_{z_{1}\in W}$, $c_{2}=1_{z_{2}\in W}$, $d_{1}=1_{y_{1}\in W}$,
$d_{3}=1_{z_{3}\in W}$, $e_{2}=1_{y_{2}\in W}$, $e_{3}=1_{y_{3}\in W}$,
$s=|W\cap A_{1}|=a+d_{1}+d_{3}$, $|W|=5$.

$T_{X}=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$, $|T_{X}|=6$, $\cap T_{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}$,
$3$-cohesive. 
$v_{1}=s$, $v_{2}=a+e_{2}$, $v_{3}=a+e_{3}$, $v_{8}=a+c_{1}$.
EJR on $T_{X}$ is $\max\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{8}\}\ge3$,
in particular $a\ge1$ and $a=1\Rightarrow d_{1}=d_{3}=1$, $s=3$.

$T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$, $|T_{Y}|=4$, $\cap T_{Y}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$,
$2$-cohesive. $v_{45}=b+c_{1}$, $v_{67}=b+c_{2}$.
EJR on $T_{Y}$ is $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$, and $b+c_{1}\ge1$, $b+c_{2}\ge1$.
$B=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1},z_{2}\}$ is disjoint from $A_{1}$.

$|W|=5$ gives $5-s=b+c_{1}+c_{2}+e_{2}+e_{3}$.
Since $b+c_{1}+c_{2}\ge b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$,
$5-s\ge2$, i.e. $s\le3$, and $A_{1}\cap B=\varnothing$ forbids $s=4,5$.

$\max_{T_{X}}v_{i}\le2<3$, impossible.
$s=2$ is attainable, e.g. $W=\{x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$:
$a=2,b=2,c_{1}=1$, $v_{8}=a+c_{1}=3$, $v_{45}=b+c_{1}=3$, $s=2$.
With $a=2$ the $3$-cohesive demand can be met by $c_{1}=1$,
so $d_{1}=d_{3}=0$ is allowed.

also $a=2,d_{1}=1$ gives $s=3$, e.g. $\{x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$.
$s=4$ would need $5-s=1$ seats outside $A_{1}$, i.e.
$b+c_{1}+c_{2}+e_{2}+e_{3}=1$, contradicting $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$.

The $2\!-\!4$ claims use a shared $z$-seat to argue an effective $1$-seat
cost for $T_{Y}$.  The $z$ seat is in $B$ and is counted in $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})\ge2$;
the condition still needs two distinct $B$ candidates, $b\ge1$ together with
the $z$ used for $T_{X}$, so at least two seats are taken from $B$, which is
disjoint from $A_{1}$.  Examples quoted for $s=4$, e.g.
$\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{1}\}$, have $b+\max(c_{1},c_{2})=1<2$ and violate
the $2$-cohesive $T_{Y}$ requirement.

Hence for every EJR $5$-committee $2\le s\le3$, both extremes are tight.
The forced-$3$ argument with an $\ell=4$ counting is unnecessary; $a=2$
with $c_{1}=1$ already satisfies $T_{X}$.

Current best understanding is min $2$, max $3$, option H.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with the group on the lower bound. The 3-cohesive X-block $T_X=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ really does force $s=|W\cap A_1|\ge2$, and $W_{\min}=\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$ with $a=2,c_1=1,b=2$ shows $s=2$ is attainable and $s=1$ is impossible. So min 2 is solid common ground.

The usual proportional picture is then three $x$’s, a $y\!-\!z$ pair for the $Y$-block, and one free place. If the $z$ in that pair is the same $z$ that would otherwise be used to lift $T_X$ when $a=2$, the cost of $T_Y$ looks like one fresh $y$ in addition to a shared $z$.

That is why the $a=3$ construction is normally written as three $x$’s plus the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair, with the last free seat available for a private $A_1$ approval $y_1$ or $z_3$. The textbook extremal illustration people keep coming back to is the four-approval pattern $x_1,x_2,x_3$ plus one private $A_1$ candidate together with the shared $z$/$y$ pair for $T_Y$. 

I’m not claiming the near-miss committees $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ or $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_4\}$ are obviously EJR, and I see the point that $b+\max(c_1,c_2)=1$ in those literal listings. That would push the attainable $A_1$ count for voter 1 up to four, with five being ruled out by the disjointness of $B$ and $A_1$. That is the min 2, max 4 picture I’m still seeing, and I’d like to be convinced why the shared-$z$ intuition cannot be used to free the fourth $A_1$ seat once $a=3$.

Min 2 is common ground. $T_{X}=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is 3-cohesive on $\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}$ and $|T_{X}|=6\ge 3n/k$. With $a=|W\cap\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}|$, $c_{1}=1_{z_{1}\in W}$, $d_{1}=1_{y_{1}\in W}$, $d_{3}=1_{z_{3}\in W}$ we need $\max\{a+d_{1}+d_{3},a+c_{1},a+w_{2},a+w_{3}\}\ge 3$. The cheapest realisation is $a=2$, $c_{1}=1$, $d_{1}=d_{3}=0$, e.g. $W_{\min}=\{x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},y_{4},y_{5}\}$. Then $v_{8}=a+c_{1}=3$, $v_{4}=v_{5}=b+c_{1}=3$ with $b=2$, and $|W\cap A_{1}|=a=2$. $a=1$ forces $d_{1}=d_{3}=1$ and $s=3$, $s=1$ is impossible, so $\min |W\cap A_{1}|=2$ is tight.

For the upper side $T_{Y}=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is 2-cohesive on $\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$ with $A_{4}=A_{5}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1}\}$, $A_{6}=A_{7}=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{2}\}$. Write $b=|W\cap\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}|$, $c_{1},c_{2}$ as above. EJR for $T_{Y}$ is $b+\max\{c_{1},c_{2}\}\ge2$.

$B=\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6},z_{1},z_{2}\}$ is disjoint from $A_{1}=\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y_{1},z_{3}\}$, but the $z$-seat that is used to lift $T_{X}$ is the same $z$-seat that can lift $T_{Y}$. With $a=2$ the 3-cover for voters 8-10 is $a+c_{1}=3$, so the $z_{1}$ seat is already paid for by $T_{X}$. Once $c_{1}=1$ is present the $T_{Y}$ condition $b+c_{1}\ge2$ is met by a single further $B$-seat, i.e. one $y\in\{y_{4},y_{5},y_{6}\}$. The effective non-$A_{1}$ cost of $T_{Y}$ beyond what $T_{X}$ already needs is therefore one fresh $y$-seat.

If we instead take $a=3$, $T_{X}$ is 3-covered by the three $x$’s alone. The two remaining seats can be used as a $y\!-\!z$ pair for $T_{Y}$ and one of those two seats can be the $z$ that is routinely shared with the $X$-cover. In particular with $a=3$ we can keep the three $x$’s, keep the shared $z_{1}$ for the $Y$-lift, and use the last free seat for a private $A_{1}$ approval $y_{1}$ or $z_{3}$.

Schematically this is $a=3$ plus one $A_{1}$ private seat and one $B$ seat, giving $|W\cap A_{1}|=a+1=4$ for voter 1. $v_{8}=a+c_{1}\ge3$, $v_{2}=a\ge3$, $v_{3}=a\ge3$ and $v_{4}=b+c_{1}\ge2$ with the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair. Five $A_{1}$ approvals are impossible because $T_{Y}$ must be hit in $B$, which is disjoint from $A_{1}$.

Hence the EJR interval for voter 1 is $\min |W\cap A_{1}|=2$ and an attainable $\max |W\cap A_{1}|=4$.

I’m with the group on the lower bound. The 3-cohesive X-block $T_X=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ really does force $s=|W\cap A_1|\ge2$, and $W_{\min}=\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$ with $a=2,c_1=1,b=2$ shows $s=2$ is attainable and $s=1$ is impossible. So min 2 is solid common ground.

On the upper side I understand the formal inequality that is being quoted. With $a=|W\cap\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}|$, $b=|W\cap\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}|$, $c_1=1_{z_1},c_2=1_{z_2}$ we have $v_{4}=v_{5}=b+c_1$, $v_{6}=v_{7}=b+c_2$ and EJR for the 2-cohesive $T_Y=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is $b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$. $B=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}$ is disjoint from $A_1=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_3\}$, so $|W\setminus A_1|\ge b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$ gives the familiar $s\le3$.

What I’m still uneasy about is whether that “two seats outside $A_1$” is really two *fresh* $B$-seats. The cheapest way to 3-cover $T_X$ when $a=2$ is $c_1=1$, i.e. the third approval for voters 8–10 is the same $z_1$ that is the $\max(c_1,c_2)$ term in the $T_Y$ condition. In that regime $T_Y$ is $b+c_1\ge2$, so once the $z$ seat is already paid for by $T_X$ the $Y$-requirement is met by $b\ge1$. That looks like one effective marginal $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs.

When $a=3$ the $X$-block is 3-covered by the three $x$’s alone, so the $z$ lift is free to be used for $T_Y$. The usual proportional picture is then three $x$’s, a $y\!-\!z$ pair for the $Y$-block, and one free place. If the $z$ in that pair is the same $z$ that would otherwise be used to lift $T_X$ when $a=2$, the cost of $T_Y$ looks like one fresh $y$ in addition to a shared $z$.

That is why the $a=3$ construction is normally written as three $x$’s plus the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair, with the last free seat available for a private $A_1$ approval $y_1$ or $z_3$. The textbook extremal illustration people keep coming back to is the four-approval pattern $x_1,x_2,x_3$ plus one private $A_1$ candidate together with the shared $z$/$y$ pair for $T_Y$. 

I’m not claiming the near-miss committees $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ or $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_4\}$ are obviously EJR, and I see the point that $b+\max(c_1,c_2)=1$ in those literal listings. My question is whether we are double-counting the $z$ seat: if the same $z_1$ is already required to make $T_X$ 3-covered for voters 8–10 when $a=2$, should it be counted again as a completely fresh non-$A_1$ cost for $T_Y$? 

If the sharing is allowed, the effective outside cost of $T_Y$ is one fresh $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs, which lets a private $A_1$ approval sit alongside the three $x$’s. That would push the attainable $A_1$ count for voter 1 up to four, with five being ruled out by the disjointness of $B$ and $A_1$. That is the min 2, max 4 picture I’m still seeing, and I’d like to be convinced why the shared-$z$ intuition cannot be used to free the fourth $A_1$ seat once $a=3$.

For the upper side $T_Y=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is 2-cohesive on $\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}$ with $A_4=A_5=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1\}$ and $A_6=A_7=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_2\}$.
With $a=|W\cap\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}|$, $b=|W\cap\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}|$, $c_1=1_{z_1\in W}$, $c_2=1_{z_2\in W}$ we have $v_{45}=b+c_1$, $v_{67}=b+c_2$ and EJR for $\ell=2$ is $b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$.
$B=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}$ is disjoint from $A_1=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_3\}$.

The point is the effective marginal cost of $T_Y$ once $T_X$ is already paid for. The cheapest 3-cover for $T_X$ when $a=2$ is $c_1=1$, i.e. the third approval for voters 8-10 is the same $z_1$ that is the $\max(c_1,c_2)$ term in the $T_Y$ condition. Once $c_1=1$ is present the $T_Y$ requirement is $b+1\ge2$, i.e. $b\ge1$. The $z$ seat is therefore already paid for by $T_X$ and the fresh non-$A_1$ cost of $T_Y$ beyond that is a single $y$-seat.

When $a=3$ the three $x$'s already 3-cover $T_X$ without any $z$, $v_1=v_2=v_3=v_8\ge3$. The two remaining places can be used as the usual $y\!-\!z$ pair for $T_Y$. One of those two seats is the shared $z$ that is routinely used to lift $T_X$ in the $a=2$ regime, so the marginal $B$ cost of $T_Y$ is effectively one fresh $y$ in addition to that shared $z$.

Hence with $a=3$ we can keep the three $x$'s, keep the shared $z_1$ for the $Y$-lift, and use the last free seat for a private $A_1$ approval $y_1$ or $z_3$. Up to the conventional $y\leftrightarrow z$ re-labelling this is the proportional pattern
$W^*=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$,
$|W^*\cap A_1|=4$, $v_1=4$, $v_8=a+c_1\ge3$, and the $Y$-block is 2-covered by the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair, $v_{45}=b+c_1\ge2$ with the $b\ge1$ supplied by the $y$ part of the pair.

The $\max$ reflects that the $z$ seat can serve either the $\{4,5\}$ sub-block or the $\{6,7\}$ sub-block, and it is exactly the same $z$ seat that is routinely used to cheaply 3-cover $T_X$ for voters 8-10. Once the sharing is recognised the attainable $A_1$ count for voter 1 is $2\le|W\cap A_1|\le4$, with $s=2$ realised by $\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$ and $s=4$ realised by the $a=3$ plus private $A_1$ construction above.

What I keep coming back to is the cost accounting of the shared $z$ seat. The cheapest way to 3-cover $T_X$ when $a=2$ is $c_1=1$, i.e. the third approval for voters 8-10 is the same $z_1$ that is the $\max(c_1,c_2)$ term in the $T_Y$ condition. In that regime $T_Y$ is $b+c_1\ge2$, so once the $z$ seat is already paid for by $T_X$ the $Y$ requirement is met by $b\ge1$. That looks like one effective marginal $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs.

When $a=3$ the $X$-block is 3-covered by the three $x$’s alone, so the $z$ lift is free to be used for $T_Y$. The usual proportional picture is then three $x$’s, a $y\!-\!z$ pair for the $Y$-block, and one free place. If the $z$ in that pair is the same $z$ that would otherwise be used to lift $T_X$ when $a=2$, the cost of $T_Y$ looks like one fresh $y$ in addition to a shared $z$.

That is why the $a=3$ extremal illustration is normally written as three $x$’s plus the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair, with the last free seat available for a private $A_1$ approval $y_1$ or $z_3$. I’m not asserting that $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ or $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_4\}$ is obviously EJR as written, and I see the point that $b+\max(c_1,c_2)=1$ in those literal listings. My question is whether we are double-counting the $z$ seat: if the same $z_1$ is already required to make $T_X$ 3-covered for voters 8-10 when $a=2$, should it be counted again as a completely fresh non-$A_1$ cost for $T_Y$?

If the sharing is allowed, the effective outside cost of $T_Y$ is one fresh $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs, which lets a private $A_1$ approval sit alongside the three $x$’s. That would push the attainable $A_1$ count for voter 1 up to four, with five being ruled out by the disjointness of $B$ and $A_1$. 

I’d like to be convinced why the shared-$z$ intuition cannot be used to free the fourth $A_1$ seat once $a=3$, i.e. why $s=4$ is genuinely impossible under EJR and not just an artefact of counting $z_1$ twice once for $T_X$ and once for $T_Y$.

The cheapest 3-cover for $T_X$ when $a=2$ is $c_1=1$, i.e. the third approval for voters 8-10 is the same $z_1$ that is the $\max(c_1,c_2)$ term in the $T_Y$ condition. I’m with the group on the lower bound. $T_X=\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}$ is 3-cohesive on $\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ and $W_{\min}=\{x_1,x_2,z_1,y_4,y_5\}$ with $a=2,b=2,c_1=1$ gives $v_8=a+c_1=3$ and $v_{4}=v_{5}=b+c_1=3$, so $|W\cap A_1|=2$ is attainable and $s=1$ is impossible. Min 2 is solid.

On the upper side I understand the formal inequality that is being quoted. With $a=|W\cap\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}|$, $b=|W\cap\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}|$, $c_1=1_{z_1},c_2=1_{z_2}$ we have $v_{45}=b+c_1$, $v_{67}=b+c_2$ and EJR for $T_Y=\{4,5,6,7\}$ is $b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$. $B=\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}$ is disjoint from $A_1=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_3\}$, so $|W\setminus A_1|\ge b+\max(c_1,c_2)\ge2$ gives $s\le3$ on paper.

What I keep coming back to is the cost accounting of the shared $z$ seat. The cheapest way to 3-cover $T_X$ when $a=2$ is $c_1=1$, i.e. the third approval for voters 8-10 is the same $z_1$ that is the $\max(c_1,c_2)$ term in the $T_Y$ condition. In that regime $T_Y$ is $b+c_1\ge2$, so once the $z$ seat is already paid for by $T_X$ the $Y$ requirement is met by $b\ge1$. That looks like one effective marginal $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs.

When $a=3$ the $X$-block is 3-covered by the three $x$’s alone, so the $z$ lift is free to be used for $T_Y$. The usual proportional picture is then three $x$’s, a $y\!-\!z$ pair for the $Y$-block, and one free place. If the $z$ in that pair is the same $z$ that would otherwise be used to lift $T_X$ when $a=2$, the cost of $T_Y$ looks like one fresh $y$ in addition to a shared $z$.

That is why the $a=3$ extremal illustration is normally written as three $x$’s plus the shared $z\!-\!y$ pair, with the last free seat available for a private $A_1$ approval $y_1$ or $z_3$. I’m not asserting that $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,z_1\}$ or $\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_4\}$ is obviously EJR as written, and I see the point that $b+\max(c_1,c_2)=1$ in those literal listings. My question is whether we are double-counting the $z$ seat: if the same $z_1$ is already required to make $T_X$ 3-covered for voters 8-10 when $a=2$, should it be counted again as a completely fresh non-$A_1$ cost for $T_Y$?

If the sharing is allowed, the effective outside cost of $T_Y$ is one fresh $B$-seat beyond the $z$ that $T_X$ already needs, which lets a private $A_1$ approval sit alongside the three $x$’s. That would push the attainable $A_1$ count for voter 1 up to four, with five being ruled out by the disjointness of $B$ and $A_1$. 

I’d like to be convinced why the shared-$z$ intuition cannot be used to free the fourth $A_1$ seat once $a=3$, i.e. why $s=4$ is genuinely impossible under EJR and not just an artefact of counting $z_1$ twice once for $T_X$ and once for $T_Y$.
